questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman sought medical advice regarding long-term antibiotic prophylaxis. She was taking benzathine penicillin G every 3 weeks. She had been diagnosed and treated for rheumatic fever when she was 15 years old after developing subcutaneous nodules, polyarthritis, and carditis. Her last echocardiogram showed no residual valvular disease.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Continue until at least age 40, and possibly lifelong
No indication for any further prophylaxis
Stop prophylaxis but give a rescue box of antibiotics for GAS pharyngitis

questions.explanation: Continue prophylaxis until age 25 All patients with rheumatic fever should receive secondary prophylaxis independent of the presence or absence of carditis and/or residual heart disease; these will only affect the DURATION of prophylaxis. The patient has known RF with carditis but no residual cardiac manifestations. In this case the recommendation is for patients to continue prophylaxis for at least 10 years from diagnosis or until age 21, whichever is longer. Since she was diagnosed at age 15, she should receive prophylaxis until age 25 which is longer than age 21. Short term duration of prophylaxis is only recommended for patients who have RF with no evidence of cardiac involvement. The recommendation to treat until age 40 or lifelong is for patients with RF with carditis and residual valvular disease, which this patient does not have. She has no indication to switch to oral antibiotics, although this could be considered. The success rates of oral prophylaxis at preventing relapse are lower than parenteral prophylaxis even with 100% adherence. Episodes of GAS pharyngitis in the patient or in household contacts should be treated promptly but not at the expense of continuing prophylaxis.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q15

questions.question: Acute rheumatic fever.

parts.text: Name 5 major criteria.
Name a minor criterion (symptom).
Name a minor criterion (laboratory).

Name two prophylactic treatment options when you have confirmed rheumatic fever without cardiac involvement.

parts_raw.text: Name 5 major criteria
Name a minor criterion (symptom)
Name a minor criterion (laboratory)
Name the essential criterion for the diagnosis
Name two prophylactic treatment options when you have confirmed RAA without cardiac involvement

questions.model_answer: a) The five major (Jones) criteria: (1) Carditis (clinical and/or subclinical/echocardiographic valvulitis) (2) Arthritis (migratory polyarthritis) (3) Sydenham chorea (4) Subcutaneous nodules (5) Erythema marginatum. b) Minor symptom criterion: arthralgia (or fever). c) Minor laboratory criterion: elevated acute-phase reactants (ESR/CRP) — or prolonged PR interval. d) Essential criterion: evidence of a preceding group A streptococcal infection (positive throat culture/rapid antigen, or an elevated/rising antistreptococcal antibody titre). e) Two prophylactic options for non-carditic disease: (1) Benzathine penicillin G 1.2 million U IM q4 weeks (2) Penicillin V 250 mg PO BID (sulfadiazine or, if penicillin-allergic, a macrolide/azalide are alternatives).

cohort_answer.text:
Five major criteria: Carditis and valvulitis (eg, pancarditis) that is clinical or subclinical; Arthritis (usually migratory polyarthritis predominantly involving the large joints); Sydenham chorea; Subcutaneous nodules; Erythema marginatum
Minor criterion (symptom): Arthralgia (if no arthritis); Fever
Minor criterion (laboratory): Elevated acute phase reactants (ESR/CRP); Prolonged PR interval
Essential criterion: Preceding GAS infection (Positive throat culture for group A beta-hemolytic streptococci, Positive rapid streptococcal antigen test, Elevated or rising antistreptococcal antibody titer)
Diagnosis notes: Two major manifestations or one major plus two minor are sufficient for diagnosis of an initial episode of ARF in a patient with evidence of a preceding GAS infection. Chorea alone is sufficient to dx ARF. Joint (arthritis or arthralgia) and cardiac (carditis or prolonged PR interval) manifestations can only be counted once, not twice, as either a major or a minor criterion. Patients with a history of ARF are at risk of subsequent episodes of ARF with GAS reinfection, and repeat episodes are associated with a greater likelihood of severe cardiac involvement. In these patients, two major, one major plus two minor, or three minor manifestations are sufficient for diagnosis of recurrent ARF.

parts.text: What are two risk factors for recurrence aside from recurrent infection?
What is the preferred agent for prophylaxis and its duration?

parts_raw.text: What are 2 risks for recurrence aside from recurrent infx?
What preffered agent for ppx and duration

questions.model_answer: a) Two factors positively correlated with rheumatic recurrence after streptococcal infection: (1) magnitude of the anti-streptolysin O (ASO) response and (2) presence of preexisting (rheumatic) heart disease. b) Preferred agent: benzathine penicillin G 1.2 million U IM every 4 weeks (every 3 weeks in high-risk settings). Duration for chorea without carditis: 5 years or until age 21, whichever is longer; if carditis with residual valvular disease, 10 years or until age 40 (sometimes lifelong).

cohort_answer.text: Risk conditions: SLE; Antiphospholipid syndrome. First line prophylaxis: IM pen G benzathine q28days or PenV. Rheumatic fever with carditis and residual heart disease - 10 years or until 40 years of age (sometimes lifelong); Rheumatic fever with carditis but no valvular disease - 10 years or until 21 years of age (whichever longer); Rheumatic fever without carditis - 5 years or 21 years of age (whichever longer)

questions.question: Acute rheumatic fever: diagnosis and prophylaxis.

parts.text: How do you diagnose acute rheumatic fever?
What is the treatment for primary and secondary prophylaxis of acute rheumatic fever?

parts_raw.text: How do you diagnose acute rheumatic fever?
B) What is the treatment for primary and secondary prophylaxis of ARF?

questions.model_answer: a) Diagnosis is clinical, using the 2015 revised Jones criteria plus evidence of a preceding GAS infection. Initial episode requires 2 major, or 1 major plus 2 minor, manifestations. Major: carditis (clinical/subclinical), arthritis, chorea, subcutaneous nodules, erythema marginatum. Minor: arthralgia, fever, elevated ESR/CRP, prolonged PR interval. Evidence of antecedent GAS infection (positive culture/rapid antigen or elevated/rising ASO or anti-DNase B) is required (except pure chorea or indolent carditis). b) Primary prophylaxis = prompt antibiotic treatment of the antecedent streptococcal pharyngitis (penicillin; per IDSA pharyngitis guidance). Secondary prophylaxis = continuous benzathine penicillin G 1.2 million U IM q4 weeks (q3 weeks high-risk), or penicillin V 250 mg PO BID, or sulfadiazine, or a macrolide/azalide if penicillin/sulfa allergic.

questions.model_answer: a) Secondary prophylaxis with benzathine penicillin G IM every 4 weeks (600,000 U if ≤27 kg, 1.2 million U if >27 kg); oral penicillin V 250 mg BID or sulfadiazine are acceptable but less effective; a macrolide/azalide if allergic to both. cohort_answer.text: 5 years from last episode of ARF OR until age 21. Prophylaxis typically involves an intramuscular injection of benzathine penicillin every 4 weeks or oral penicillin V twice daily. Sulfadiazine or oral macrolides for penicillin allergy. Current AHA guidelines no longer recommend bacterial endocarditis prophylaxis for patients with rheumatic heart disease, unless prosthetic valve.
